opus-5.5.text:
The thing that really struck us when we started running these virtual lab meetings is just how compressed the timeline becomes. In a human research setting, if you want to bring together, say, an immunologist, a computational biologist, and a machine learning person to brainstorm a project, you have to coordinate calendars, and realistically that meeting might happen in a week or two. Then there's follow-up, someone writes notes, and the next meeting is another couple of weeks out. So one cycle of ideation and critique can take a month.

With the virtual agents, a full meeting, where each agent proposes ideas, a critic agent pushes back, and the principal investigator agent synthesizes a decision, takes a few minutes. And it costs very little in compute. That changes the way you can do research in a qualitative way, not just a quantitative way.

One thing it enables is running many meetings in parallel. We can ask the same question five separate times, let the agents discuss independently, and then have another meeting where they merge the best ideas across those runs. That's something you'd never do with human teams because it would be an enormous waste of people's time. But with agents, it actually gives you more robust conclusions, because you can see which ideas keep coming up and which ones were just one-off suggestions.

The speed also means you can iterate much more aggressively. If the agents design a pipeline and a step doesn't work, they can reconvene right away, diagnose the issue, and try a different approach. In our nanobody design work, for instance, the agents went from setting the overall strategy to choosing the tools and writing the code very quickly, and then we as humans could focus our time on the part that really needs us, which is running the experiments in the wet lab and checking whether the designs actually bind.

I'd also say the speed lowers the stakes of exploring unconventional ideas. When a meeting is expensive, people tend to be conservative and stick with what they know. When it's nearly free, you can afford to explore a weird direction, see if it holds up under critique, and discard it if it doesn't. So I think the real value isn't just doing the same science faster. It's that it shifts the human role toward setting good questions, giving high-level guidance, and doing validation, while the agents handle a lot of the rapid back-and-forth in between.

r001.rationale: The response says agent meetings take a few minutes and can be run in parallel, including five independent runs. It does not state that agents can conduct hundreds of meetings during the time humans spend on one meeting’s preliminaries.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the speed is one of the most underappreciated aspects of the whole thing. When you have human research collaborators, a project meeting happens maybe once a week, sometimes once every two weeks. People have to find time on their calendars, somebody is traveling, somebody has a grant deadline. So the actual cadence of iteration on an idea is quite slow, even if everyone involved is brilliant.

With the virtual agents, a "meeting" between, say, the immunologist agent, the computational biologist agent, and the machine learning agent takes a few minutes. They propose ideas, critique each other, revise, and converge. And then you can run that again immediately. So instead of one round of feedback per week, you can get dozens of rounds in an afternoon. That compounds. Ideas that would have taken months to refine through back-and-forth can get sharpened very quickly.

The other thing I find valuable is that the speed changes how you, as the human, engage with the process. Because each round is cheap, you can be much more exploratory. You can say, let's try framing the problem three different ways and see which one the team gravitates toward, and that's a reasonable thing to do rather than an imposition on a bunch of busy people. It lowers the cost of a bad idea, which honestly makes you more willing to put ideas on the table.

And I'd add that fast doesn't mean the output is shallow. A lot of the quality comes from the critic role, where an agent is specifically tasked with pushing back on the proposals. Because the loop is fast, you can afford many rounds of critique and revision, which is often where the real improvement happens. In a human meeting, that critique phase gets compressed because everyone wants to wrap up. Here it doesn't have to be.

r001.rationale: The response says agent meetings take a few minutes and allow dozens of feedback rounds in an afternoon, but it does not state that agents can hold hundreds of meetings during the time humans spend on a single meeting’s preliminaries.

astra-6.text: What’s valuable is how quickly you can iterate. A meeting between virtual agents can happen in a few seconds or minutes, so you can look at the ideas they generate, give feedback, and have them reconvene. With human collaborators, that same cycle might take days just because of scheduling. That speed lets you explore more possibilities, identify weaknesses earlier, and bring the most promising ideas back to people for deeper discussion.

r001.rationale: The response says virtual-agent meetings take seconds or minutes and contrasts that with human scheduling taking days, but it does not state that agents can hold hundreds of meetings during the preliminaries for one human meeting.

sol-6.1.text: What I find valuable is how quickly you can iterate. A group of virtual agents can have a discussion in a few minutes, and then you can look at what they produced, give feedback, and have them meet again. With human collaborators, scheduling that next meeting might take days or weeks. So the benefit isn’t just that one meeting is faster—it’s that you can go through many more cycles of proposing ideas, critiquing them, and refining them.
